sections.title: How are various parts connected in our body?
Can we control movement in our body?
How does the body sense, communicate and respond?

slides.title: Connective Tissue Connects
slides.kicker: Blood aur bone, dono body ke connectors!
bullets: A tissue that connects and supports other tissues is called a connective tissue.
Blood and bone are both connective tissues, yet blood is fluid while bone is hard.
The difference lies in the matrix: watery and jelly-like in blood, hard and rigid in bone.

left.title: Blood
items: Matrix is watery, soft and jelly-like

right.title: Bone
items: Matrix is hard, solid and rigid

slides.title: Inside Your Blood
slides.kicker: Laal rang ka raaz yahin hai!
bullets: The red colour of blood comes from haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in the Red Blood Cells.
RBCs live for about 4 months and are replaced regularly.
Plasma makes up 55 per cent of blood volume; formed elements make up the other 45 per cent.
Platelets help in blood clotting at the site of an injury.
slides.note: RBC ki expiry: chaar mahine, phir naye!

slides.title: Blood Stories Daily
slides.kicker: Daud ke baad chehra laal kyun?
bullets: When you get a small cut, red blood oozes out and a clot forms after some time.
A skin injury turns the area red and slightly swollen, sometimes with fever.
While running, muscles need more oxygen, so breathing becomes faster and blood flow increases.
White Blood Cells collect at infected areas, causing pus, redness and swelling.

slides.title: Bone, Cartilage, Ligament
bullets: Bone has a rigid matrix containing calcium and phosphorus, giving strength, support and protection.
Touch your elbow gently: you feel a hard and rigid structure at work.
Cartilage cushions the ends of bones, absorbing shocks.
Table 3.4 and Fig. 3.12 list bone, cartilage and ligament among the connective tissues of the body.

slides.title: Voluntary or Involuntary
bullets: Movements like lifting objects are voluntary: you decide them on purpose.
Voluntary movements are carried out by skeletal muscles, which are attached to the skeleton.
Involuntary movements happen automatically, like food moving in the intestine and the beating of the heart.
slides.note: Digestion rukti nahi, aap bina bole!

slides.title: Skeletal Muscle Story
bullets: Skeletal muscles are made of bundles of long, cylindrical cells called muscle fibres.
The fibres are unbranched and multinucleate, meaning they have many nuclei.
They are striated, showing light and dark bands.

slides.title: Smooth Muscle Steady
bullets: Smooth muscles are found in organs like the stomach and intestines.
Their cells are spindle shaped, with a single nucleus, and they lack striations.
They help in slow, continuous movements like digestion, without any conscious control.

slides.title: Cardiac Muscle Never Tires
bullets: Cardiac muscles are found only in the heart.
Their fibres are cylindrical and branched, with a single nucleus and faint striations.
They work tirelessly and rhythmically, so the heart beats throughout life without fatigue.
slides.note: Ek hi kaam, poori zindagi, bina thake!

slides.title: The Control Network
bullets: Nervous tissue forms the body's control and coordination network.
The brain acts as the control centre, coordinating activities, memory and responses.
Muscles, voluntary or involuntary, cannot function independently; they receive instructions from nervous tissue.
During exercise, the brain signals the heart to beat faster to meet the body's increased need for oxygen.

slides.title: Meet the Neuron
bullets: The cells of nervous tissue are called neurons, or nerve cells.
Neurons are specialised to receive, process and transmit messages.

slides.title: Three Parts, One Message
bullets: The cell body contains the nucleus and controls the cell's activities.
Dendrites receive signals coming from other neurons.
The axon is a long fibre that carries messages away and ends at axon terminals.
Axon terminals transmit the messages on to other cells.
slides.note: Dendrite sunta hai, axon bhejta hai!

slides.title: Framework That Moves
bullets: The musculoskeletal system is made up of bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments.
It helps us stand upright, move, and protects delicate organs.
The whole system functions under the control of the nervous system.

slides.title: How Muscles Move Bones
bullets: Muscles pull on bones to produce movement.
Tendons are strong, flexible bands that attach muscles to bones.
When a muscle contracts, the tendon transmits this force to the bone.
The result is movement at a joint.

slides.title: How Heavy Is Your Skeleton
bullets: On average, the adult human skeleton makes up about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight.
This can vary with age, gender and body composition.
Activity 3.4: multiply your weight by the bone and muscle percentages to estimate each one.
Book averages: adult males about 40 to 50 per cent muscle, adult females about 30 to 40 per cent.

slides.title: Move and Observe
bullets: Activity 3.5 asks you to move different parts of your body and watch what each can do.
Some parts move easily in many directions, while others move only in a single direction.
The difference is due to the types of joints present in each place.

slides.title: What Is a Joint
bullets: A joint is a junction between two or more bones.
Joints allow movement, but they cannot move the bones on their own.
Bones actually move when muscles pull on them.

slides.title: Stem Cells, Fresh Starts
bullets: Bone marrow contains special cells that can divide and make new cells.
In a bone marrow transplant, stem cells from a healthy person are given to a patient.
This helps patients with blood cancers like Leukemia and disorders such as Thalassemia.
slides.note: Ek healthy insaan, ek nayi shuruaat!

slides.title: Shoulder, Movement Champion
bullets: The shoulder joint allows free movement of the arm.
The rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone.
This arrangement is called the ball and socket joint.

slides.title: The Shoulder Girdle
slides.kicker: Arm ko jodta hai skeleton se!
bullets: Together with the collarbone, the shoulder forms the shoulder girdle.
The shoulder girdle connects the arm to the skeleton.
The book shows this joint in Fig. 3.16.

slides.title: Four Ways to Swing
bullets: The ball and socket joint allows forward, backwards, sideways and circular movements.
That is why the arm can swing freely in every direction.
Try it now: move your arm forward, backward, sideways and in a full circle.

slides.title: Skull, A Hard Case
bullets: The skull is a hard case of flat bones joined together.
It protects the brain, eyes and ears.
Guarding the brain is the skull's most important work.

slides.title: Fixed Means Fixed
bullets: The bones of the skull are connected by fixed joints.
Fixed joints mean the skull bones cannot move.
This keeps the brain safe even when the body moves.
slides.note: Kabhi socha, skull kyun naache na?

slides.title: Dance Poses Detective
bullets: Fig. 3.17 shows poses of classical and folk dances of India.
Look carefully at each pose and identify which joints are involved.
For every joint you spot, work out what type of movement it allows.
Fixed joints like those of the skull stay still, while other joints create the poses.

slides.title: Bones That Guard
bullets: The skeletal system is a framework of bones that provides strength and protects delicate internal organs.
It includes the skull, the vertebral column and the rib cage.

slides.title: The Amazing Spine
slides.kicker: Bend karo, twist karo, safe raho!
bullets: From the base of the skull extends a flexible column called the backbone, or vertebral column.
It is made of a series of small bones called vertebrae and helps us stand upright.
Between each vertebra sits a cartilage disc, which acts as a cushion.
These discs allow flexibility, so we can bend and twist without injuring the spinal cord.

slides.title: A Cage That Breathes
bullets: You have 12 pairs of ribs; together they form a protective cage around the heart and lungs.
Ribs attach to the spine at the back and to the breast bone, the sternum, in front.
Flexible cartilage joins them, so the cage expands and contracts during breathing.
This movement moves air in and out of the lungs; rib injuries can make breathing painful.

slides.title: Yoga, A Gift
bullets: Yoga, described in ancient Indian texts, includes physical postures and breathing practices.
It reduces stress and helps prevent lifestyle diseases.
The book also underlines correct posture, proper nutrition, regular exercise and yoga.
Every year, 21st June is observed as International Yoga Day; Fig. 3.18 shows poses of Surya Namaskar.

slides.title: One Cell, Whole Plant
bullets: In 1958, F. C. Steward showed that single cells from the phloem of a carrot can regrow whole plants.
He grew the cells in a nutrient medium containing simple sugars and hormones.
The cells first dedifferentiated, regaining the ability to divide into an unspecialised mass.
With nutrients and growth chemicals, the mass divided and differentiated into a complete plant.
slides.note: Totipotency: ek cell se poora paudha!

flashcards.front: What is a connective tissue?
flashcards.back: A tissue that connects and supports other tissues. Blood and bone are both connective tissues.

flashcards.front: Blood is fluid but bone is rigid. What makes the difference?
flashcards.back: The matrix: it is watery, soft and jelly-like in blood, and hard, solid and rigid in bone.

flashcards.front: Which blood components clot a cut and fight infection?
flashcards.back: Platelets help clot blood at the injury site; White Blood Cells gather at infected areas, causing pus, redness and swelling.

flashcards.front: What makes blood red, and how long do RBCs live?
flashcards.back: Haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in Red Blood Cells. RBCs live about 4 months and are replaced regularly.

flashcards.front: What are voluntary movements? Name the muscles.
flashcards.back: Movements done by conscious choice, like lifting objects. Skeletal muscles attached to the skeleton carry them out.

flashcards.front: Describe skeletal muscle fibres.
flashcards.back: Long, cylindrical cells in bundles; unbranched, multinucleate and striated with light and dark bands.

flashcards.front: Where are smooth muscles found and what is their job?
flashcards.back: In organs like the stomach and intestines; they make slow, continuous movements like digestion, involuntarily.

flashcards.front: What is special about cardiac muscle?
flashcards.back: It is found only in the heart. Its branched fibres beat tirelessly and rhythmically all through life, without fatigue.

flashcards.front: What does nervous tissue do in the body?
flashcards.back: It forms the body's control and coordination network; the brain coordinates activities, memory and responses.

flashcards.front: What is a neuron?
flashcards.back: A nerve cell, specialised to receive, process and transmit messages. Neurons are the cells of nervous tissue.

flashcards.front: Name the three main parts of a neuron.
flashcards.back: The cell body with its nucleus, dendrites that receive signals, and an axon ending in axon terminals.

flashcards.front: Why does the heart beat faster during exercise?
flashcards.back: The brain signals the heart to beat faster to meet the body's increased demand for oxygen.

flashcards.front: Which parts make up the musculoskeletal system?
flashcards.back: Bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments.

flashcards.front: What is a tendon?
flashcards.back: A strong, flexible band that attaches a muscle to bone and transmits the muscle's pull when it contracts.

flashcards.front: What fraction of adult body weight is the skeleton?
flashcards.back: About 12 to 15 per cent, though it varies with age, gender and body composition.

flashcards.front: Who controls the musculoskeletal system?
flashcards.back: The nervous system controls it. Muscles pull on bones to produce movement.

flashcards.front: Define joint.
flashcards.back: A junction between two or more bones. Joints allow movement but cannot move the bones on their own.

flashcards.front: Why does the shoulder move many ways but other parts less freely?
flashcards.back: Because the range of movement depends on the type of joint present at that place.

flashcards.front: What are stem cells?
flashcards.back: Special cells that can divide and make new cells. Bone marrow contains them.

flashcards.front: Which diseases can bone marrow transplants help treat?
flashcards.back: Blood cancers like Leukemia and disorders such as Thalassemia, using stem cells from a healthy person.

flashcards.front: What fits into what in a ball and socket joint?
flashcards.back: The rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone.

flashcards.front: Which movements does the shoulder joint allow?
flashcards.back: Forward, backwards, sideways and circular movements.

flashcards.front: What is the shoulder girdle?
flashcards.back: The shoulder together with the collarbone; it connects the arm to the skeleton.

flashcards.front: Which joints join the skull bones?
flashcards.back: Fixed joints, so the skull bones cannot move at all.

flashcards.front: Why is it good that skull bones cannot move?
flashcards.back: The fixed joints keep the brain safe and protected, even when the body moves.

flashcards.front: Which organs does the skull protect?
flashcards.back: The brain, eyes and ears, inside a hard case of flat bones.

flashcards.front: Name the three main parts of the skeletal system.
flashcards.back: The skull, the vertebral column (backbone or spine) and the rib cage.

flashcards.front: What sits between two vertebrae and what does it do?
flashcards.back: A cartilage disc, which acts as a cushion and allows flexibility, protecting the spinal cord as we bend and twist.

flashcards.front: How many pairs of ribs do we have?
flashcards.back: 12 pairs. They form the rib cage, a protective cage for the heart and lungs.

flashcards.front: Who showed that one carrot cell can regrow a whole plant?
flashcards.back: F. C. Steward in 1958, using single phloem cells grown in a nutrient medium with sugars and hormones.

flashcards.front: How does the rib cage help you breathe?
flashcards.back: Ribs joined by flexible cartilage let the cage expand and contract, moving air in and out of the lungs.

quiz.why: Fig. 3.12a shows plasma is 55 per cent of total volume and formed elements are 45 per cent.

quiz.why: Formed elements are 45 per cent of volume, and 45 per cent of 200 mL is 90 mL.

quiz.why: Skeletal muscles attached to the skeleton carry out voluntary movements.

quiz.q: A muscle cell is spindle shaped with a single nucleus and no striations. Where is it from?
quiz.why: Smooth muscle in organs like the stomach has spindle-shaped cells, one nucleus and no striations.

Flat cells, no nuclei, no striations

quiz.why: Nervous tissue controls actions like pulling your hand away from something hot, with the brain as control centre.

quiz.q: Which part of a neuron receives signals from other neurons?
quiz.why: Dendrites receive signals; the axon carries messages away to the axon terminals.

Dendrites, cell body, axon, axon terminals
Axon terminals, axon, cell body, dendrites

quiz.why: The book says the musculoskeletal system functions under the control of the nervous system.

quiz.q: Tendons attach
quiz.why: Muscles are attached to bones by strong, flexible bands called tendons.

quiz.q: A 40 kg adult's skeleton weighs closest to
quiz.why: The skeleton is about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight; 12 to 15 per cent of 40 kg is 4.8 to 6 kg.

quiz.q: A joint is a junction between
quiz.why: The book defines a joint as a junction between two or more bones.

quiz.q: Joints allow movement, but what actually moves the bones?
quiz.why: Joints cannot move the bones on their own; muscles pull on bones to produce movement.

quiz.q: Which statement about joints is true?
options: They allow movement but cannot move bones on their own
They are made of striated fibres
Every joint moves in one direction only
quiz.why: Joints allow movement but cannot move the bones on their own; the joint type decides the range.

quiz.q: Which joint lets the arm move forward, backward, sideways and in circles?
quiz.why: The ball and socket joint of the shoulder allows forward, backwards, sideways and circular movements.

quiz.q: In a ball and socket joint, the rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into
options: a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone
a deep socket of the hip bone

quiz.q: The shoulder girdle, which connects the arm to the skeleton, is formed by
options: the upper arm bone and ribs
quiz.why: Together with the collarbone, the shoulder forms the shoulder girdle.

quiz.q: The bones of the skull are connected by
quiz.why: Skull bones are connected by fixed joints, so they cannot move.

quiz.q: Why do skull bones not move?
options: They are joined by fixed joints
quiz.why: Fixed joints connect the skull bones, keeping them still so the brain stays safe.

quiz.q: A dancer swings her arm and bends her neck, yet her skull stays rigid. Why?
options: Skull bones meet at fixed joints
quiz.why: Fixed joints keep the skull bones still, protecting the brain even when the body moves.

quiz.q: How many pairs of ribs form the human rib cage?
quiz.why: The book states we have 12 pairs of ribs, joined to the spine and sternum, forming the rib cage.

quiz.q: What lies between each vertebra and lets the spine bend safely?
quiz.why: A cartilage disc acts as a cushion between vertebrae and allows flexibility.

quiz.q: In front, the ribs are attached to the
quiz.why: Ribs attach to the spine at the back and to the breast bone, the sternum, in front.

options: Dedifferentiated and regained the power to divide
quiz.why: Phloem cells first dedifferentiated into an undifferentiated mass, then grew into a complete plant.

examples.title: Fractions of Blood in a Bag
examples.problem: A blood donation bag holds 400 mL of blood. Using the components of blood from Fig. 3.12a, find how much of it is plasma and how much is formed elements.
steps: Plasma makes up 55 per cent of total blood volume, and formed elements make up 45 per cent.
Plasma: 55 per cent of 400 mL = 400 x 55/100 = 220 mL.
Formed elements: 45 per cent of 400 mL = 400 x 45/100 = 180 mL.
examples.answer: The bag holds 220 mL of plasma and 180 mL of formed elements.

examples.title: Weighing Your Skeleton
examples.problem: Activity 3.4: Aditi records her total body weight as 40 kg. Estimate the weight of her bones and her muscles using the book's averages.
steps: The adult skeleton is about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight.
Bone weight: 12 per cent of 40 = 4.8 kg, and 15 per cent of 40 = 6 kg. So her bones weigh about 4.8 to 6 kg.
For muscle, the book gives adult males about 40 to 50 per cent and adult females about 30 to 40 per cent.
Taking 30 to 40 per cent for her: 12 to 16 kg of muscle.
Compare these values with classmates and calculate the class average, as the activity suggests.
examples.answer: Her bones weigh about 4.8 to 6 kg and her muscles about 12 to 16 kg of her 40 kg body weight.

examples.title: Name That Muscle
examples.problem: A microscope slide shows three muscle samples. A has long, unbranched, multinucleate striated fibres. B has spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus and no striations. C has branched, cylindrical fibres with one nucleus and faint striations. Identify each sample and say whether it works voluntarily.
steps: Sample A: unbranched, multinucleate, striated fibres match skeletal muscle, which is attached to the skeleton.
Skeletal muscle carries out voluntary movements like lifting objects, so A works under conscious control.
Sample B: spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus and no striations match smooth muscle of organs like the stomach and intestines; it moves food during digestion involuntarily.
Sample C: branched cylindrical fibres with faint striations match cardiac muscle, found only in the heart, beating rhythmically without fatigue.
examples.answer: A is skeletal muscle (voluntary), B is smooth muscle (involuntary) and C is cardiac muscle (involuntary).

examples.title: From One Carrot Cell to a Plant
examples.problem: Describe, step by step, how F. C. Steward's 1958 experiment turned single carrot phloem cells into complete plants, and state what the experiment proves.
steps: Steward took single cells from the vascular phloem of a carrot and cultured them in a nutrient medium containing simple sugars and hormones.
The phloem cells first dedifferentiated: they regained the ability to divide and formed an undifferentiated mass of unspecialised cells.
Grown with nutrients and growth chemicals under appropriate conditions, the cells of the mass divided and differentiated further.
The mass gradually developed into a complete plant.
examples.answer: Single carrot phloem cells are totipotent: they can regenerate a whole plant, which Steward first demonstrated in 1958.
